title_original: Paris Photo and the Pictet Prize : An Interview with Valérie Belin
excerpt_original: As the new official partner of Paris Photo, the Prix Pictet honours Alfredo Jaar and Valérie Belin. An interview with the photographer who won the prize in 2015. Cet article Paris Photo and the Pictet Prize : An Interview with Valérie Belin est apparu en premier sur The Eye of…

blocks.text: As a new official partner of Paris Photo, the Prix Pictet, dedicated to photographic work addressing environmental issues, will present works by two of its previous winners, Alfredo Jaar and Valérie Belin, at the Grand Palais from November 12 to 15. An interview with the photographer Valérie Belin who won the prize in 2015 for her series Still Life .

Still Life was created in 2014. In this series, you revisit the traditional genre of still life through compositions of mass-produced consumer objects, particularly plastic ones. How did the series come about?

In my work, I have always alternated between portraits and photographs of objects. I wanted to transpose the traditional genres of still life and vanitas into a contemporary setting, that of mass consumption and overconsumption.

Just before this series, I had photographed collectors’ interiors (the Interiors series, editor’s note), where people had accumulated so many objects in their homes that they were completely overwhelmed by them. I wanted to assemble my own collections, creating large-scale vanitas compositions strongly inspired by painting and the tradition of elaborate seventeenth-century still lifes. I began looking for ordinary contemporary objects, things with no particular qualities. Quite intuitively, I started buying enormous quantities of objects from discount shops in Paris.
I arranged and assembled them on a table, taking photographs at each stage as the objects accumulated. In a sense, the right photograph was the one taken just before the entire arrangement collapsed.
There is a striking contrast between the classical tradition of still life and the contemporary objects you depict.

The compositions are carefully constructed and elaborate. Through this contrast, we realise that whereas still-life painting represented real things meat, fruit, flowers everything here has become useless, artificial, reduced to a kind of simulacrum.

At the time, I even used the term “refuse” to describe these objects, because they were outside the world: they had lost their practical value and had been reduced to decoration. This is something that often appears in my work, where the human figure itself can be treated as part of the setting, as an object.

There has been a gradual progression in my work, from subjects that genuinely existed towards increasingly virtual subjects whose reality could ultimately be questioned. From bodybuilders to shop-window mannequins, which already represented a first step towards these dematerialised subjects, whose reality becomes uncertain.

In an earlier interview, you explained that working in colour allowed you to go further in exploring the “unreality” of your work. In Still Life, you alternate between colour and black-and-white images. What motivated this choice?
It was very meaningful to me, particularly in terms of the evolution of photography. With the advent of digital photography, the choice between colour and black and white can now be made afterwards.

The black-and-white compositions thus acquire a more abstract quality. Black and white removes the colour differences that distinguish the objects from one another. This was important to me because it also reinforced the destructive quality of these compositions: everything dissolves, the elements merge with one another. There is a kind of disappearance of representation through this process. For the colour images, I worked by subtracting colour. I added flat areas and colour gradients, rather like a painter establishing the local colour of a painting.

Still life is, in a sense, a non-subject, a minor genre within the hierarchy of subjects in painting and photography. The emphasis is therefore placed on representation itself. One thinks of Manet’s asparagus, where you can sense the sheer pleasure he took in painting it, the sensuality of the brushwork. It is painting in its purest form. Something similar happened for me. I experimented with every possibility of altering the colours. It was as though I had painted my photographs.
Twelve years after creating the series, how do you view Still Life today?

The subjects remain relevant. The production of useless objects is not declining. They continue to be manufactured, creating an entirely parallel universe. It is as though they were immortal, as though they were the ones destroying us. The underlying questions raised by the series have not disappeared.
You won the Prix Pictet in 2015 with this series, an award recognising photographic work that contributes to social and environmental debate. What do you remember about that moment?

It is an unforgettable memory. I wasn’t expecting it at all. I didn’t think my work was sufficiently politically correct to be selected. I felt an immense sense of joy. Kofi Annan himself presented me with the prize, which was very moving. When I first started photography, I could never have imagined experiencing anything like that.

It was also a tremendous recognition of all the people who had supported me, both on the jury and throughout those years of work. I think it is a very important prize, one that consolidates a career and strengthens the confidence of institutions and collectors.
The theme of the 2015 Prix Pictet was “Disorder”. How did Still Life relate to this notion of disorder?

I do think this series addresses a form of disorder, or perhaps a new world order. There is always a head at the centre of the compositions. It is something of a metaphor for a disturbed mind. Fragments of bodies emerge from this mass, and the human figure becomes an object among others. There is a kind of contamination between the human and the object.
The following year, you experienced the Prix Pictet from the other side, as a member of the jury. What did you take away from that experience?

Once again, it was an extremely enriching experience. I had to select portfolios that I would then defend before the jury’s deliberations. It was an opportunity to discover certain bodies of work, but also to meet the other members of the jury. All those exchanges, the discussions about why we favoured one submission over another, were fascinating.

It also meant meeting collectors and people with a genuine passion for photography. I got to know Martin Barnes better, and he became a very important figure for me because he truly supported my work. In particular, he organised an exhibition at the Victoria and Albert Museum following the Prix Pictet. I owe all of that to the prize.

Still Life will be one of the two series presented at the Grand Palais as part of the inaugural exhibition marking the partnership between the Prix Pictet and Paris Photo. Your photographs will be shown alongside Alfredo Jaar’s landscapes from The End, a series devoted to the disappearance of the Great Salt Lake in Utah. What connections do you see between your respective approaches?

We have quite different working methods and aesthetics. Alfredo Jaar’s approach is somewhat more conceptual than mine. I really like this series of photographs. There is something mysterious and irreducible about them. It is not work that can be reduced to a message or a critique of our society. The images also have a life of their own, an element of mystery that persists beyond any interpretation. That is very close to my own way of working.

We have never met, and I find it interesting to see how the public will perceive this juxtaposition. I will be presenting three images: one very large black-and-white photograph and two colour images. The presentation is quite concentrated, simple and restrained. Opposite them will be Alfredo Jaar’s photographs. It is interesting to bring together two bodies of work that are almost diametrically opposed in their approaches, yet ultimately converge in what they evoke.
